paragraphs: The upper floor had a number of large rooms that were kept purely for show and furnished in the old-fashioned merchant style. Dull, long rows of clumsy mahogany chairs stood against the walls, glass chandeliers hung under covers, and gloomy mirrors hung on the walls. None of these rooms were ever used. The old man lived in one small, remote bedroom, where an old servant woman with a kerchief on her head looked after him, along with a lad who sat on the chest out in the passage. His legs were so swollen that he could barely walk. Only now and then was he lifted out of his leather armchair, and then the old woman held him up and walked him once or twice up and down the room. He was sullen and silent even with her.

When he was told that the “captain” had come, he refused flatly to see him. Mitya would not give up and sent up his name a second time. Samsonov questioned the lad closely. What did the man look like? Was he drunk? Would he make a scene? The answer was that he was sober, but he would not leave. The old man refused again. Mitya had expected this and had brought pencil and paper on purpose. He now wrote in a clear hand, “On most important business closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna,” and sent the note up.

Samsonov thought it over for a little. Then he told the lad to show the visitor into the drawing-room, and sent the old woman downstairs to tell his younger son to come up at once. This son was over six feet tall and uncommonly strong. He was clean-shaven and dressed in the European fashion, though his father still wore a kaftan and a beard. He came immediately and said nothing. The whole family trembled before the father. The old man had called for this giant, not because he was afraid of the “captain” (he was not at all a timid man), but to have a witness if anything went wrong. Leaning on his son and the servant lad, he waddled at last into the drawing-room. We may suppose he was very curious. The room where Mitya waited was vast and dreary, and it pressed down on the spirits. It had a double row of windows, a gallery, marbled walls, and three huge chandeliers hung with glass drops and covered with shades.

Mitya sat on a little chair near the entrance, waiting for his fate in nervous impatience. When the old man came in at the far door, seventy feet away, Mitya sprang up and went to meet him with his long, military stride. He was well dressed, in a buttoned-up frock-coat, with a round hat and black gloves in his hands. It was just how he had looked three days before at the elder’s, at the family meeting with his father and brothers. The old man stood waiting for him, dignified and unbending, and Mitya felt at once that the old man had looked him through and through as he came forward. He was also struck by Samsonov’s monstrously swollen face. The lower lip, always thick, now hung down like a bun. The old man bowed to his guest in dignified silence and waved him to a low chair by the sofa. Then, leaning on his son’s arm, he started to lower himself onto the sofa opposite, groaning with pain. Watching his struggle, Mitya at once felt remorse. He felt, too, how small he was in the presence of this dignified man he had dared to disturb.
“What do you want from me, sir?” said the old man, slowly, distinctly, sternly, but with courtesy, once he was finally seated.

Mitya jumped, leapt to his feet, then sat down again. Straight away he began to speak, loudly, in nervous haste, waving his arms, in a real frenzy. Anyone could see he was a man cornered, on the edge of ruin, clutching at his last straw and ready to go under if it failed him. Old Samsonov probably understood all this in an instant, though his face stayed as cold and still as a statue’s.

“Most honored sir, Kuzma Kuzmitch, you have surely heard more than once of my quarrels with my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who robbed me of my inheritance from my mother ... seeing the whole town is gossiping about it ... for here everyone gossips about things they shouldn’t ... and besides, it might have reached you through Grushenka ... Sorry, through Agrafena Alexandrovna ... Agrafena Alexandrovna, the lady I hold in the highest respect and esteem ...”

So Mitya began, and he broke down at the very first sentence. We will not give his speech word for word, only the gist. Three months ago, he said, he had gone to a lawyer in the chief town of the province, “of express intention” (Mitya deliberately used these words in place of “intentionally”). “A distinguished lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmitch, Pavel Pavlovitch Korneplodov. Perhaps you’ve heard of him? A man of vast intellect, the mind of a statesman ... he knows you, too ... spoke of you in the highest terms ...” Mitya broke down again. But these breakdowns never stopped him. He took a leap across each gap and struggled on and on.

This Korneplodov had questioned him closely and looked over the documents he could bring (Mitya referred to these documents rather vaguely and hurried past the subject). He had then reported that they could certainly bring a suit over the village of Tchermashnya, which should have come to him, Mitya, from his mother, and so checkmate the old villain, his father ... “because not every door was shut, and justice might still find a loophole.” In short, he could count on another six or even seven thousand roubles from Fyodor Pavlovitch, because Tchermashnya was worth at least twenty-five thousand, he might say twenty-eight thousand, in fact “thirty, thirty, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would you believe it, I didn’t get even seventeen out of that heartless man!” So he, Mitya, had dropped the matter for the moment, since he knew nothing about the law. But when he came here, a counter-claim against him left him dumbstruck (here Mitya lost his way again and again took a flying leap ahead). “So won’t you, excellent and honored Kuzma Kuzmitch, agree to take over all my claims against that unnatural monster, and pay me a lump sum of only three thousand?... You see, there’s no way you can lose by it. On my honor, my honor, I swear it. Quite the opposite, you could make six or seven thousand instead of three.” Above all he wanted it settled that very day.

“I’ll do the business with you at a notary’s, or wherever it’s done ... in fact, I’m ready to do anything.... I’ll hand over all the deeds ... whatever you want, I’ll sign anything ... and we could draw up the agreement right now ... and if it were possible, if it were only possible, this very morning.... You could pay me that three thousand, for there isn’t a capitalist in this town to compare with you, and so you would save me from ... save me, in fact ... for a good, I might say an honorable deed.... For I have the most honorable feelings for a certain person you know well, and look after like a father. I wouldn’t have come at all, if it weren’t as a father. And really, it’s a struggle of three in this business, for it’s fate—that’s a fearful thing, Kuzma Kuzmitch! A tragedy, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a tragedy! And since you dropped out long ago, it’s a tug-of-war between two. I’m putting it awkwardly, perhaps, but I’m not a literary man. You see, I’m on one side, and that monster on the other. So you must choose. It’s either me or the monster. It all lies in your hands—the fate of three lives, and the happiness of two.... Forgive me, I’m making a mess of it, but you understand ... I can see from your venerable eyes that you understand ... and if you don’t understand, I’m done for ... so you see!”

With that “so you see!” Mitya cut short his clumsy speech. He jumped up from his seat and waited for an answer to his foolish proposal. At that last phrase, he had suddenly realized, with despair, that it had all fallen flat, and above all that he had been talking utter nonsense.

“How strange! On the way here it seemed all right, and now it’s nothing but nonsense.” The thought dawned on his despairing mind all at once. The whole time he had been speaking, the old man had sat without moving, watching him with an icy look in his eyes. He kept Mitya in suspense for a moment. Then Kuzma Kuzmitch said, in the flattest and most chilling tone:
“Excuse me, we don’t take on such business.”
Mitya suddenly felt his legs going weak under him.
“What am I to do now, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” he muttered, with a pale smile. “It’s all up with me, I suppose—what do you think?”
“Excuse me....”
Mitya stayed on his feet, staring, unable to move. Then he noticed a stir in the old man’s face. He started.
“You see, sir, business of that kind isn’t in our line,” said the old man slowly. “There’s the court, and the lawyers—it’s pure misery. But if you like, there’s a man here you could go to.”
“Good heavens! Who is it? You’re my salvation, Kuzma Kuzmitch,” faltered Mitya.

“He doesn’t live here, and he isn’t here at the moment. He’s a peasant, and he deals in timber. His name is Lyagavy. For the past year he’s been haggling with Fyodor Pavlovitch over your copse at Tchermashnya. They can’t settle on a price, maybe you’ve heard? He’s back again now, and he’s staying with the priest at Ilyinskoe, about twelve versts from the Volovya station. He wrote to me about the copse as well, and asked my advice. Fyodor Pavlovitch means to go and see him himself. So if you got there before Fyodor Pavlovitch and made Lyagavy the offer you’ve made me, he might possibly—”

“A brilliant idea!” Mitya broke in, ecstatic. “He’s just the man, it would suit him perfectly. He’s haggling over it, they’re asking him too much, and here he’d be getting all the papers that give him title to the property itself. Ha ha ha!”
And Mitya suddenly let out his short, wooden laugh, which made Samsonov start.
“How can I thank you, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” cried Mitya, gushing.
“Don’t mention it,” said Samsonov, with a nod of his head.
“But you don’t know, you’ve saved me. Oh, it was a true presentiment that brought me to you.... So now, off to this priest!”
“There’s no need to thank me.”
“I’ll make haste and fly there. I’m afraid I’ve worn out your strength. I’ll never forget this. A Russian is telling you that, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a R-r-russian!”
“Of course!”
Mitya reached out and seized his hand to shake it, but a spiteful gleam showed in the old man’s eye. Mitya drew back his hand, then at once scolded himself for his distrust.
“It’s because he’s tired,” he thought.

“For her sake! For her sake, Kuzma Kuzmitch! You understand that it’s for her,” he cried, and his voice rang through the room. He bowed, spun around, and with the same long stride went to the door without looking back. He was trembling with joy.

“Everything was on the edge of ruin, and my guardian angel has saved me,” he thought. If a businessman like Samsonov (a most worthy old man, and what dignity!) had suggested this way out, then ... then success was certain. He would fly off at once. “I’ll be back before night, I’ll be back tonight and it will be done. Could the old man have been laughing at me?” cried Mitya, as he strode toward his lodging. He could think of nothing else, of course, except that this was practical advice, “from such a businessman,” who knew the business and who knew this Lyagavy (curious name!). Or else the old man was laughing at him.

Alas! It was the second. Long afterward, when the catastrophe had happened, old Samsonov himself admitted, with a laugh, that he had made a fool of the “captain.” He was a cold, spiteful, sarcastic man, with a streak of violent dislikes. Maybe it was the “captain’s” excited face. Maybe it was the foolish certainty of this “rake and spendthrift” that Samsonov could be taken in by a cock-and-bull story like his scheme. Maybe it was jealousy over Grushenka, in whose name the “scapegrace” had burst in on him with such a tale, to get money. Something worked on the old man, but I can’t say what. But at the moment when Mitya stood before him, feeling his legs go weak and crying wildly that he was ruined, the old man looked at him with intense spite and made up his mind to turn him into a laughing-stock. When Mitya had gone, Kuzma Kuzmitch, white with rage, turned to his son and ordered him to see that the beggar was never seen again, and never let into the yard, or else he’d—

He did not say what he would do. But even his son, who often saw him in a rage, shook with fear. For a whole hour afterward the old man trembled with anger, and by evening he was worse and sent for the doctor.
